newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK futures chief Riley says China won't meddle.
newsitem.headline: HK futures chief Riley says China won't meddle.

text.p: Hong Kong's outgoing futures exchange chief said he believed China's regulatory authorities would not interfere should a Hong Kong exchange be faced with a crisis when under Chinese rule.
"In our particular industry if anything major did happen, I don't think there would be any tendency on their part to step in," said Ivers Riley, chairman of the Hong Kong Futures Exchange Ltd.
"I think some people within the (Chinese) bureaucracy might think in those terms, but I think their leadership would keep that from happening."

Riley, 65, said he delayed his retirement in the territory until the end of 1997 instead of 1996 because he had been so positive about the outlook for Hong Kong after it reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on Monday, June 30.
Riley will retire in December and be succeeded by Robert Gilmore, previously with Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission.
"What was happening was we were getting a lot of growth automatically, but also we were building up for all the opportunities here to come after the changeover," said Riley.
This was chiefly because of China's economic growth phase, he said.

"We see ourselves as being the international outlet from the standpoint of the futures industry, and we see a lot of things that China is going to need that will have us involved," Riley said. "So, I wanted to be here as that all starts."
Riley said Chinese regulatory authorities recognised the two areas were in very different phases of development.
"In our particular industry they are on a major programme of limiting the industry, standardising it and reducing the players," Riley said.
"At the same time we are in an all-out growth pattern, expanding international linkages. They know that full well, they are happy to see it," he added.
The exchange linked up with the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) on June 13. This allowed Hong Kong futures exchanges direct access to NYMEX's futures and options markets.
The exchange will relaunch trading in interest rate futures in September and plans to launch another futures contract on an equity index in the Asia region, Riley said.
On the mainland, Chinese regulatory authorities wanted to see controlled growth in the industry, he said.
"When I say controlled growth, what I am talking about is regulated," he said. "Six years ago in China there was no futures law, and there were zero futures exchanges."
"Three years ago there was no futures law and 52 futures exchanges, and this year in China there is still no futures law and there are 14 exchanges," he said

A futures law was being drafted and would bring "standardisation or professionalisation" to the industry and most likely cut the number of commodities futures exchanges in China to less than 10, he said.
"They are going to end up with fewer exchanges and fewer companies and they are going to have less state company involvement," said Riley.
"When they finish all of that they will have a pretty good base."
